A technique, apparatus, and arrangement are provided for identifying and responding to an actual or impending runaway event in a diesel engine system. The system has an intake that delivers combustion air to the diesel engine and an exhaust that carries exhaust gases away from the engine. It also includes an exhaust gas recirculation arrangement configured to selectively route exhaust gas from the exhaust side back into the intake side. A first gas-flow-path actuator is positioned in the exhaust gas recirculation arrangement, while a second gas-flow-path actuator is positioned in the exhaust.

In operation, the system detects a present or possible runaway condition. When such a condition is detected, the system reacts by reducing the oxygen available to the diesel engine. This oxygen deprivation is carried out by opening the first gas-flow-path actuator and closing the second gas-flow-path actuator, thereby causing the diesel engine to stall. The oxygen reduction is achieved by maximizing the return of exhaust gases to the engine and raising the pressure drop across the exhaust for a first preset duration.

The invention relates to a method, device, and system for detecting and counteracting a runaway condition in a diesel engine system. A runaway condition may occur when a diesel engine begins operating in an uncontrolled manner, for example by continuing to accelerate or sustain combustion independently of normal fuel control. Because a diesel engine can continue running as long as sufficient combustible material and oxygen are available, the invention provides a way to stop or prevent such operation by reducing the oxygen available for combustion.

The diesel engine system includes an inlet configured to supply combustion air to the engine and an exhaust configured to discharge exhaust gas from the engine. The system further includes an exhaust gas recirculation system that connects the exhaust side of the engine to the inlet side. Through this exhaust gas recirculation system, at least a portion of the exhaust gas can be redirected from the exhaust back into the intake airflow. The recirculated exhaust gas has a lower oxygen content than fresh air and can therefore be used to reduce the oxygen concentration entering the engine.

The system is configured to detect an actual or potential runaway condition in the diesel engine. Detection may be based on operating parameters such as engine speed, acceleration, fuel command, intake conditions, exhaust conditions, or other indicators suggesting that the engine is operating or may begin operating outside normal controlled limits. Once such a condition is identified, the system initiates a countermeasure intended to rapidly reduce the engine’s ability to continue combustion.

In response to detecting the runaway condition, the system deprives the diesel engine of oxygen in order to cause the engine to stall. This is accomplished by controlling components in the exhaust and exhaust gas recirculation paths. In particular, an exhaust gas recirculation actuator is opened to increase the flow of exhaust gas from the exhaust side back to the inlet side, while an exhaust actuator is closed to restrict the discharge of exhaust gas from the engine. These actions maximize exhaust gas recirculation and increase the pressure drop in the exhaust system, thereby promoting the flow of oxygen-depleted exhaust gas into the engine inlet.

The exhaust gas recirculation actuator is held open and the exhaust actuator is held closed for a predetermined period of time. During this period, the proportion of recirculated exhaust gas supplied to the engine increases, while the supply of fresh oxygen-rich combustion air is reduced. As a result, the oxygen concentration available in the combustion chambers falls to a level insufficient to sustain combustion, causing the diesel engine to stall. In this way, the invention provides an effective response to an actual or potential diesel engine runaway condition by using the exhaust gas recirculation system and exhaust flow control to suppress combustion and bring the engine to a stop.
outputs.L4:
A diesel engine runaway detection and mitigation system is designed to identify and respond to an actual or potential runaway condition in which the engine begins operating uncontrollably, often because it is consuming an unintended fuel source such as oil mist, crankcase vapors, or combustible gases present in the intake air. In such a condition, simply reducing or shutting off the normal fuel supply may not be sufficient to stop the engine, because the engine may continue to receive combustible material from another source. The system therefore uses components associated with the exhaust and exhaust gas recirculation system to limit the oxygen available for combustion and bring the engine to a controlled stop.

The system includes one or more sensors or control inputs capable of detecting conditions that indicate an actual or impending runaway event. These conditions may include engine speed exceeding a predetermined threshold, a rapid unintended acceleration of the engine, a mismatch between commanded fueling and observed engine output, abnormal intake or exhaust conditions, or other operating parameters suggesting that the engine is not responding normally to control commands. When the control system determines that a runaway condition exists or is likely to occur, it initiates a mitigation strategy intended to deprive the engine of sufficient oxygen to sustain combustion.

To carry out this strategy, the system controls an exhaust gas recirculation actuator and an exhaust flow actuator. The exhaust gas recirculation actuator may be a valve or similar device that regulates the flow of exhaust gas from the exhaust system back into the intake system. The exhaust flow actuator may be a valve, throttle, brake valve, variable geometry turbocharger mechanism, or other device capable of restricting exhaust flow downstream of the engine. Under normal operating conditions, these actuators may be positioned to support emissions control, engine braking, turbocharger operation, or general engine performance. During a runaway mitigation event, however, the control system commands the actuators to positions that maximize the amount of exhaust gas returned to the intake and increase the restriction in the exhaust path.

In particular, the system opens the exhaust gas recirculation actuator to allow a large volume of exhaust gas to flow into the intake stream. Exhaust gas contains significantly less oxygen than fresh intake air and includes combustion products that dilute the incoming charge. By recirculating as much exhaust gas as possible, the system reduces the oxygen concentration available in the cylinders. At the same time, the system closes or substantially restricts the exhaust flow actuator. This increases the exhaust pressure upstream of the restriction and creates a higher pressure differential that promotes exhaust gas recirculation through the recirculation path. The increased exhaust pressure and reduced exhaust outlet flow also impose additional pumping losses on the engine.

The combined effect of opening the recirculation path and restricting the exhaust outlet is to flood the intake with low-oxygen exhaust gas while increasing the resistance against which the engine must operate. As the oxygen content of the intake charge falls, combustion becomes weak, unstable, or impossible to sustain. The added exhaust backpressure further loads the engine and reduces its ability to continue running. Together, these effects cause the engine speed to decrease and ultimately stall, stopping the runaway condition without relying solely on cutting off the commanded fuel supply.

This approach provides a controlled method for shutting down a diesel engine during runaway operation. Rather than allowing the engine to overspeed until mechanical failure occurs, the system actively changes the air and exhaust flow conditions to suppress combustion. The mitigation strategy may be implemented automatically by an electronic control unit, and it may also be coordinated with other shutdown measures, such as disabling fuel injection, closing an intake throttle if available, activating warning indicators, or recording diagnostic information. By using existing exhaust gas recirculation and exhaust restriction hardware, the system can provide a rapid and effective response to runaway conditions while reducing the likelihood of catastrophic engine damage.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical description of a method, device, and system for counteracting runaway in a diesel engine by maximizing exhaust gas recirculation and increasing exhaust backpressure.
counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Description: Method, Device, and System for Counteracting Runaway in a Diesel Engine

### 1. Technical Field

The disclosure relates to diesel engine safety control systems and, more particularly, to a method, device, and system for counteracting a diesel engine runaway condition by increasing exhaust gas recirculation flow and increasing exhaust backpressure to reduce oxygen availability and engine breathing efficiency.

---

### 2. Background

A diesel engine may enter a runaway condition when it continues to accelerate or operate despite a reduction or cessation of commanded fueling. Such a condition may be caused by unintended combustible material entering the intake stream, such as lubricating oil vapor, crankcase fumes, turbocharger seal leakage, or external hydrocarbon vapor. Because diesel engines regulate output primarily by fuel quantity rather than intake throttling, simply reducing injected fuel may not immediately stop combustion if an alternative fuel source is present.

Known shutdown systems may include intake air shutoff valves or fuel cutoff strategies. However, in some applications it is desirable to provide an additional or alternative runaway mitigation strategy using existing exhaust gas recirculation and exhaust aftertreatment hardware. By maximizing exhaust gas recirculation and increasing exhaust backpressure, the oxygen concentration of the intake charge may be reduced and the pumping losses of the engine may be increased, thereby reducing combustion intensity and engine speed.

---

### 3. Summary

A method for counteracting runaway in a diesel engine includes detecting an engine runaway condition, commanding an exhaust gas recirculation valve to a maximum-flow or substantially maximum-flow position, and commanding an exhaust restriction device to increase exhaust backpressure. The increased exhaust gas recirculation displaces oxygen in the intake charge with inert exhaust constituents, while the increased exhaust backpressure reduces engine scavenging efficiency and increases pumping work. In combination, these actions counteract the runaway condition by reducing the amount of oxygen available for combustion and by applying a load to the engine.

A device according to the disclosure includes an electronic controller configured to receive engine operating signals, determine the presence of a runaway condition, and output control commands to an exhaust gas recirculation actuator and an exhaust backpressure actuator. The exhaust backpressure actuator may be associated with an exhaust throttle valve, variable geometry turbocharger, exhaust brake, wastegate, aftertreatment flow restrictor, or other controllable exhaust restriction device.

A system according to the disclosure includes a diesel engine having an intake passage, an exhaust passage, an exhaust gas recirculation passage fluidly connecting the exhaust passage to the intake passage, an exhaust gas recirculation valve arranged in the exhaust gas recirculation passage, an exhaust backpressure device arranged in or coupled to the exhaust passage, and a controller configured to implement a runaway mitigation control mode.

---

### 4. System Architecture

The system may include:

1. **Diesel engine**
   - A compression ignition internal combustion engine having one or more cylinders, an intake manifold, and an exhaust manifold.

2. **Intake system**
   - An intake passage configured to deliver charge air to the engine.
   - Optionally, an intake throttle or air shutoff valve.

3. **Exhaust system**
   - An exhaust passage configured to receive exhaust gas from the engine.
   - Optionally, a turbocharger turbine, aftertreatment components, muffler, or exhaust brake.

4. **Exhaust gas recirculation system**
   - An EGR passage connecting the exhaust side to the intake side.
   - An EGR valve configured to regulate recirculated exhaust flow.
   - Optionally, an EGR cooler and EGR bypass passage.

5. **Exhaust backpressure device**
   - A controllable restriction configured to increase pressure in the exhaust passage.
   - The device may include one or more of:
     - an exhaust throttle valve,
     - an exhaust brake valve,
     - a variable geometry turbocharger turbine actuator,
     - a turbocharger wastegate actuator,
     - a controllable aftertreatment restriction,
     - a flap valve or butterfly valve in the exhaust conduit.

6. **Controller**
   - An engine control unit or dedicated safety controller.
   - Configured to receive sensor inputs and issue actuator commands.

7. **Sensors**
   - Engine speed sensor.
   - Accelerator pedal or operator demand sensor.
   - Fuel injection command or delivered fuel estimate.
   - Intake manifold pressure sensor.
   - Exhaust manifold pressure sensor.
   - EGR differential pressure or EGR flow sensor.
   - Intake oxygen sensor, lambda sensor, or mass airflow sensor.
   - Crankcase pressure sensor or turbocharger speed sensor, where available.

---

### 5. Runaway Detection

The controller may determine that a runaway condition exists when one or more operating parameters indicate that engine speed or torque is inconsistent with commanded fueling or operator demand.

A runaway condition may be detected based on at least one of the following:

- engine speed exceeding a predetermined threshold;
- engine speed increasing at a rate greater than a predetermined acceleration threshold;
- engine speed remaining above an idle or commanded-speed range despite reduced or zero fuel command;
- measured intake airflow or manifold pressure inconsistent with commanded operating state;
- torque estimate exceeding expected torque for a commanded fuel quantity;
- turbocharger speed exceeding a threshold;
- abnormal intake oxygen, exhaust oxygen, or lambda value;
- detection of hydrocarbon vapor or oil mist in the intake stream;
- failure of engine speed to decrease following commanded fuel cutoff.

In one implementation, runaway is detected when the controller commands zero or near-zero injected fuel and engine speed continues to increase or remains above a calibrated threshold for a calibrated time interval.

---

### 6. Runaway Mitigation Control Mode

Upon detection of runaway, the controller enters a runaway mitigation mode. In this mode, the controller may perform one or more of the following actions:

1. **Maximize EGR flow**
   - Command the EGR valve to a fully open or maximum permissible position.
   - Open an EGR cooler bypass or select a flow path that maximizes recirculated exhaust delivery.
   - Adjust turbocharger geometry or exhaust pressure to promote EGR flow from exhaust to intake.
   - Reduce intake oxygen concentration by displacing intake air with recirculated exhaust gas.

2. **Increase exhaust backpressure**
   - Command an exhaust throttle, exhaust brake, or exhaust restriction device toward a closed or restrictive position.
   - Adjust a variable geometry turbocharger to a high-backpressure position.
   - Close or partially close a wastegate if doing so increases exhaust manifold pressure.
   - Increase pumping losses and reduce engine breathing efficiency.

3. **Coordinate EGR and backpressure**
   - Increase exhaust pressure upstream of the EGR tap to drive EGR flow into the intake.
   - Maintain sufficient pressure differential across the EGR valve to maximize recirculated exhaust flow.
   - Avoid actuator positions that would damage hardware or exceed calibrated pressure limits.

4. **Reduce or cease injected fuel**
   - Command fuel injection quantity to zero or a minimum safe value.
   - Disable pilot, main, and post injections where possible.

5. **Optional intake restriction**
   - Close an intake throttle or air shutoff valve if present.
   - Use intake restriction in combination with EGR and exhaust backpressure to further reduce oxygen availability.

6. **Operator and diagnostic actions**
   - Activate a warning lamp, audible alarm, or remote alert.
   - Store a diagnostic trouble code.
   - Log engine speed, sensor values, and actuator positions.
   - Prevent restart until a service reset or inspection occurs.

---

### 7. Control Strategy

The controller may execute a closed-loop strategy to maximize inert gas fraction in the intake while constraining pressure and temperature limits.

An example control sequence includes:

1. Monitor engine speed, fuel command, intake pressure, exhaust pressure, and EGR position.
2. Determine whether runaway criteria are satisfied.
3. If runaway is detected, command fuel cutoff.
4. Command the EGR valve to a maximum open position.
5. Command the exhaust backpressure device toward a restrictive position.
6. Monitor exhaust manifold pressure and intake manifold pressure.
7. Adjust the exhaust restriction to maintain exhaust backpressure below a maximum allowable pressure.
8. Maintain maximum EGR flow until engine speed drops below a calibrated safe threshold or the engine stops.
9. Keep the system in a locked shutdown or post-event safety state until reset.

The controller may prioritize exhaust backpressure control according to a pressure limit. For example, the exhaust restriction device may be closed until exhaust pressure reaches a calibrated upper limit, after which the restriction is modulated to maintain the pressure near the limit without exceeding it.

Similarly, the EGR valve may remain fully open unless intake pressure, EGR cooler temperature, or other system protection limits require modulation.

---

### 8. Device Description

A runaway mitigation device may include:

- a processor;
- memory storing instructions executable by the processor;
- input circuitry configured to receive engine operating data;
- output circuitry configured to command an EGR valve actuator and an exhaust backpressure actuator.

The memory may store instructions that cause the processor to:

1. determine a runaway state based on engine speed and fuel command;
2. generate a maximum-EGR command;
3. generate an increased-backpressure command;
4. coordinate the commands to reduce intake oxygen concentration and increase engine pumping losses;
5. maintain the commands until engine speed is reduced below a threshold or the engine stops.

The device may be integrated into an engine control module, aftertreatment control module, vehicle control unit, generator control unit, marine engine controller, or industrial engine safety controller.

---

### 9. Method Description

A method for counteracting runaway in a diesel engine may comprise:

1. sensing an operating parameter of the diesel engine;
2. determining, using a controller, that the diesel engine is operating in a runaway condition;
3. commanding an exhaust gas recirculation valve toward a maximum-flow position;
4. commanding an exhaust backpressure device toward a restrictive position;
5. increasing exhaust manifold pressure to promote exhaust gas recirculation into an intake passage;
6. reducing an oxygen concentration of an intake charge delivered to the diesel engine;
7. increasing pumping losses of the diesel engine by restricting exhaust flow;
8. maintaining the EGR and exhaust backpressure commands until engine speed decreases below a predetermined value or engine operation ceases.

The method may further include ceasing commanded fuel injection, closing an intake throttle, activating an alarm, storing diagnostic information, and preventing restart until inspection.

---

### 10. Example Implementation

In an example diesel engine equipped with high-pressure EGR and an exhaust brake, a controller monitors engine speed and commanded fuel quantity. If the controller commands zero fuel but engine speed continues to rise above a calibrated speed threshold, the controller determines that a runaway event is occurring.

The controller immediately commands the EGR valve fully open and commands the exhaust brake valve toward a closed position. Closing the exhaust brake increases exhaust manifold pressure upstream of the EGR port. The higher exhaust pressure drives exhaust gas through the fully open EGR valve into the intake manifold. The recirculated exhaust gas contains a lower oxygen concentration than fresh air and includes combustion products such as carbon dioxide and water vapor. The resulting intake mixture supports less combustion of unintended fuel. At the same time, the exhaust restriction increases pumping work required to expel exhaust gases from the cylinders. These combined effects reduce engine speed and oppose the runaway condition.

The exhaust brake may be modulated to avoid exceeding a maximum allowable exhaust manifold pressure. The EGR valve may remain fully open until engine speed falls below a safe threshold or the engine stops.

---

### 11. Variations

The system may be adapted to engines having:

- high-pressure EGR;
- low-pressure EGR;
- dual-loop EGR;
- variable geometry turbocharging;
- exhaust brakes;
- turbo-compounding;
- aftertreatment devices with controllable flow restriction;
- stationary generator sets;
- marine propulsion engines;
- mining, oilfield, agricultural, construction, or on-road vehicles.

In a variable geometry turbocharger implementation, the controller may command turbine vanes to a position that increases exhaust manifold pressure while also promoting EGR flow. In a dual-loop EGR system, the controller may command both high-pressure and low-pressure EGR valves to maximum or calibrated maximum positions.

---

### 12. Advantages

The disclosed method, device, and system may provide one or more of the following advantages:

- rapid reduction of intake oxygen concentration;
- increased engine braking and pumping losses;
- use of existing EGR and exhaust brake hardware;
- complementary operation with fuel cutoff and intake shutoff systems;
- improved mitigation of runaway caused by unintended fuel sources;
- controller-based automated response without requiring operator intervention;
- applicability to mobile, stationary, industrial, and marine diesel engines.

counterfactuals.output:
In one embodiment, a diesel engine system comprises an internal combustion diesel engine having an air inlet and an exhaust outlet, an exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) passage fluidly coupling the exhaust outlet to the air inlet, a first gas flow actuator disposed in or associated with the EGR passage, and a second gas flow actuator disposed in or associated with an exhaust passage downstream of the exhaust outlet. The first gas flow actuator is operable to selectively permit or restrict recirculation of exhaust gas from the exhaust outlet to the air inlet, and the second gas flow actuator is operable to selectively permit or restrict discharge of exhaust gas through the exhaust passage.

The system further comprises a controller configured to detect, determine, or receive an indication of a diesel engine runaway condition. In response to the detected runaway condition, the controller is configured to command the first gas flow actuator to an open position, thereby increasing exhaust gas recirculation to the air inlet, and to command the second gas flow actuator to a closed position, thereby restricting exhaust flow from the exhaust outlet through the exhaust passage. The controller maintains the first gas flow actuator in the open position and the second gas flow actuator in the closed position for a predetermined time period.

During the predetermined time period, recirculated exhaust gas is directed from the exhaust outlet through the EGR passage to the air inlet, while discharge of exhaust gas through the exhaust passage is restricted. The resulting reduction in oxygen concentration available for combustion in the diesel engine inhibits continued uncontrolled combustion and thereby mitigates or terminates the runaway condition. Upon expiration of the predetermined time period, the controller may return the first gas flow actuator and the second gas flow actuator to respective non-runaway operating positions or to other positions selected according to engine shutdown or recovery control logic.
